text_blocks.snippet: Treatment options for high blood pressure (hypertension) include heart-healthy lifestyle modifications and prescription medications, as outlined by the Mayo Clinic and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.

snippet_links.text: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

snippet_highlighted_words: heart-healthy lifestyle modifications and prescription medications

list.snippet: DASH Diet: Eat a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on saturated fat.
Sodium Reduction: Limit daily sodium intake to 1,500 mg or less (or under 2,300 mg maximum).
Physical Activity: Get about 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (such as brisk walking) per week.
Weight Management: Lose or maintain a healthy body weight if you are overweight.
Habits: Quit smoking, limit alcohol consumption, manage chronic stress, and get 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night.

text_blocks.snippet: Doctors often prescribe one or more of these standard drug classes, detailed by the American Heart Association:

list.snippet: ACE Inhibitors: Help blood vessels relax and widen (e.g., Lisinopril, Enalapril).
Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Block chemicals that constrict blood vessels, often preferred to protect the kidneys (e.g., Losartan, Valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel cells to lower pressure (e.g., Amlodipine, Diltiazem).
Thiazide Diuretics: "Water pills" that help the body get rid of excess sodium and water (e.g., Chlorthalidone, Hydrochlorothiazide).
Beta-Blockers: Often used if you have coexisting heart conditions, heart failure, or arrhythmias (e.g., Metoprolol, Carvedilol).
Other Agents: Alpha-blockers, central-acting agents, or vasodilators may be added if blood pressure remains uncontrolled.
Multidrug Regimens: Stage 2 hypertension often requires a combination of two or more medications, sometimes available in a single daily pill.
